> Electrotrack is a multi-stage electromagnetic ball accelerator (coilgun) with a custom PCB. An ESP32 reads IR photo-interrupters along a 3D-printed track and fires a sequence of coils to pull a steel ball forward. Each coil is switched off as the ball reaches its center, so it isn't pulled back. Hardware - ESP32 controller, 4 coil channels (logic-level N-MOSFETs + flyback diodes) - Coils wound from 0.3 mm copper wire - 3S LiPo (≈12 V)  - IR position sensors salvaged from a photocopier - 7.5 mm or 12 mm steel ball [final choice TBD] Status - Concept, hand-drawn schematic, KiCad schematic,  idea reel done  - Next: BOM, PCB layout - Later: coil winding, 3D-printed track, firmware, speed measurement - GitHub: The repository will contain the KiCad project, BOM, and firmware. *Inspired by Hyperspace Pirate's electromagnetic accelerator project.*

### Day 1 (05.10, 4:00pm–9:00pm): Ideas, decisions and schematic

**How it started**
I watched Hyperspace Pirate's video *"Electromagnetic Accelerator Improvements Part II"* and realized that building something similar was well within reach. That's when I decided to make it my Half-Life project, featuring a custom PCB to control the system.

> *Inspiration: Hyperspace Pirate's Electromagnetic Accelerator project*
![inspiration](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/D1H5wjMaoqfsZfeTslugwWB4nIQcEzNR/229890c17214dee5c3dc695fed51462b1cc270b4c3bc81aaf889bd493b4f221c.jpg)

**Design decisions**

- **Power:** 3S LiPo battery (already on hand).
- **Coils:** Wound from 0.3 mm copper wire (plenty available). Planning 4 coils for the initial setup.

> *Coils match-cut*
![coils](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/D1H5wjMaoqfsZfeTslugwWB4nIQcEzNR/71cedc5ea22cd10fc80464ccd9d67abb825a0e5668672fb1b5a6fdf055d60a76.gif)

> *0.3 mm copper wire spool and 3S LiPo battery*
![wire and battery](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/D1H5wjMaoqfsZfeTslugwWB4nIQcEzNR/1b4818696516cfcd65c9d9b305f46254e9cbe6af19df525b42753f2ee66ec82e.jpeg)

- **Projectile:** Found two steel balls (7.5 mm and 12 mm). Testing both to determine the optimal choice.

> *Candidate projectiles: 7.5 mm and 12 mm steel balls*
![Projectile](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/D1H5wjMaoqfsZfeTslugwWB4nIQcEzNR/af06d2e8b73eb9ff7e527acea8892c0e2878ffcb147529d9b1676d1299a14ed2.jpeg)

- **Mechanics:** 3D-printed guide track and structure.
- **Controller:** ESP32 microcontroller instead of a purely analog timing circuit. It provides precise timing control and allows dedicated firmware development.

> *ESP32 microcontroller board match-cut*

- **Sensors:** Salvaged IR photo-interrupters from an old photocopier, eliminating the need to purchase new sensors.

> *IR sensors match-cut*
![IR](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/D1H5wjMaoqfsZfeTslugwWB4nIQcEzNR/068eac135437a217ea9e9b019de667c8a639f1ed608a0acf771ed3847d246c86.gif)

> *Close-up of the salvaged IR sensor components*

**Schematic**
I carefully drew the complete circuit by hand on paper (~3 hours including research): featuring an ESP32, 4 MOSFET channels, coil drivers with flyback diodes, IR position sensors, and power regulation (12 V input to L7805 5 V regulator feeding the ESP32 VIN). The rest of the afternoon was spent refining decisions and recording footage for the video reel.

> *Drafting the circuit schematic by hand*
![drawing](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/D1H5wjMaoqfsZfeTslugwWB4nIQcEzNR/6afd34f153f555bcad915ce59f7bc9067bcb158de39e4ea21b4971c7ef149735.gif)

> *Completed hand-drawn schematic diagram*
![schematic](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/D1H5wjMaoqfsZfeTslugwWB4nIQcEzNR/f7ba8cd80ad2b3ba156fc6c0146ebd6b72a234233b0c6e983505987c3b2d455c.jpeg)

**Problems & Solutions**

- **Bare IR sensors:** They consist only of raw IR LEDs and phototransistors. Added 220 Ω current-limiting resistors for LEDs and 10 kΩ external pull-up resistors for phototransistors, as ESP32 input-only pins lack internal pull-ups.
- **Powering ESP32 from 12 V:** Lacking a buck converter, I utilized an L7805 linear regulator. Heat dissipation will be managed with a small heatsink.
- **ESP32 pin selection:** Avoided strapping pins during boot and mapped all IR sensor inputs to dedicated input-only pins (GPIs).

### 2026-10-11 – Week 1 – Entry 2: KiCad schematic, PCB layout and routing

**9.18h**

Week 1 – Entry 2: KiCad schematic, PCB layout and routing
Total time: ~7.2 h (recorded in timelapses)

* ~3 h: KiCad schematic, footprints and BOM
* ~2 h: component placement + OLED and spare-GPIO headers
* ~1 h: routing the 2-layer board
* ~1 h: DRC fixes, Gerber/BOM export and GitHub repo
* ~1 h: editing the timelapse reel & writing Entry 2

Day 3 (07.10): KiCad schematic, footprints and BOM
I redrew the hand-drawn schematic in KiCad: ESP32 30-pin devkit, 4 coil channels (IRLZ44N MOSFET, 100 ohm gate resistor, 10k pull-down, SB560 flyback diode), 4 IR sensor inputs (JST XH connectors with resistors), 12 V input through an XT30 connector with fuse and switch, and an L7805 for 5 V.

![schematic](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/D1H5wjMaoqfsZfeTslugwWB4nIQcEzNR/3b39a14ae5428734f6d433e6eb5703f1005094a694422dabb4213581d63f6829.png)

KiCad schematic

Then I assigned footprints and exported the BOM.

![footprint](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/D1H5wjMaoqfsZfeTslugwWB4nIQcEzNR/3065b54ca51a5a8df67fa0073e07a85f3dae258c72068315989d50682df1c4ff.png)

Footprints assigned and loaded into the PCB editor

Day 4 (08.10): Component placement
I placed all components on the board, then added two extras: a 0.96" I2C OLED header (SDA on GPIO21, SCL on GPIO22) to show ball speed, and a 1x10 header with spare GPIOs, 3.3 V and GND for future needs.

Day 5 (10.10): Tidying the layout
I regrouped the parts: each coil channel in one row (terminal, flyback diode, MOSFET, resistors), power input and capacitors in one corner, ESP32 with the USB port at the board edge, and IR connectors on the opposite side.

Day 6 (11.10): Routing, DRC and fabrication files
I routed a 2-layer board: 2.5 mm traces for 12 V, 1.5-2.5 mm for coil nets, 0.3-0.5 mm for signals, and a GND copper pour on both layers. Then I ran DRC and fixed all errors (thermal relief errors solved with solid pad connections, plus one unconnected GND pad). Only silkscreen warnings are left. Finally I exported Gerbers, drill files, BOM and schematic, and pushed everything to GitHub.

![3d](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/D1H5wjMaoqfsZfeTslugwWB4nIQcEzNR/86fe5185d5067398fa694d7c6ad49d3f62786b66d3601bcc5b141c53852f79a0.png)

3D view of the finished PCB

Problems & Solutions

* Wrong layer count: the imported JLCPCB template had 4 copper layers. I switched the board to 2 layers in Board Setup.
* XT30 polarity: the + and - were swapped between my schematic and the footprint. I fixed it in the schematic before routing.
* MOSFET gate drive: the IRLZ44N gate is driven from 3.3 V, but the datasheet specifies its on-resistance only for 4-5 V. I decided to keep it for this version and measure the drain-source voltage when I build it. A gate driver can be added later if needed.
* DRC errors: the GND pour used a 0.5 mm clearance and thermal reliefs, which left some pads under-connected. Changing it to a 0.3 mm clearance and solid pad connections fixed all errors.
* Gate and pull-down resistors (open item from Entry 1): chose 100 ohm gate resistors and 10k pull-downs, so the MOSFETs stay off while the ESP32 boots.
* IR LED resistors: the schematic uses 150 ohm from 3.3 V (about 14 mA, assuming about 1.2 V forward voltage) instead of the 220 ohm I first planned. I will verify this with the real sensors.

Still to check / Next steps

* Measure the coil DC resistance and check that the 5 A fuse matches the peak current.
* Measure the MOSFET drain-source voltage with a 3.3 V gate drive during a coil pulse.
* Check how hot the L7805 gets.
* Firmware must limit the on-time of each coil.
* Order the PCB and parts after approval, wind the coils and 3D-print the track.
